o.notes: The clip consists of a single open back unrounded vowel [ɑː], which corresponds to the British English letter name for 'R' as well as the word 'are'.

t.notes: Extremely short, isolated voiceless alveolar plosive release/burst without any voiced vowel or recognizable lexical word.

p.notes: A voiceless velar plosive followed by an added schwa, typical of an isolated phonics pronunciation of the consonant sound for 'c' or 'k'.

i.notes: A clear British pronunciation of the English letter name 'K'.

b.notes: A clear pronunciation of the English letter name 'T' (homophonous with the word 'tea') by a British speaker.

k.notes: Isolated voiceless bilabial plosive [p] with a short burst of aspiration, without a voiced vowel or the letter name /piː/.

g.notes: A short voiced bilabial nasal hum [m] with no preceding or following vowel; not the letter name 'em'.

d.notes: A very brief voiceless bilabial plosive release (aspirated 'p'), not the letter name 'pee' and not a full word.

r.notes: A long close back rounded vowel [uː], functioning as the exclamation 'ooh'.

u.notes: A single open back unrounded vowel [ɑː], corresponding to the British English pronunciation of the letter 'R' or the word 'are'/'ah'.

j.notes: A clear pronunciation of the British English letter name 'R' (or the homophonous word 'are').

ch.notes: The clip contains only the voiceless postalveolar affricate consonant [tʃ], with no following vowel, letter name, or lexical word.

ks.notes: An isolated voiceless velar plosive with aspirated release, not pronounced as a letter name or full word.

h.notes: A very short isolated British English short vowel sound [ʌ], typically used for the phonics sound of the letter 'u' (as in 'up' or 'umbrella'), or possibly the filler particle 'uh'.

kw.notes: A short isolated voiceless velar plosive [kʰ], representing the phonics sound of the letter C or K rather than the letter name.

ou.notes: A clear, single-syllable pronunciation of the English word 'how' with an aspirated glottal fricative onset and diphthong [aʊ].

oo.notes: An isolated long close back rounded vowel [uː], commonly heard as the exclamation 'ooh'.

schwa.notes: A single open vowel sound [ɑː], identical in British English to the letter name 'R' as well as words like 'are' and 'ah'.

air.notes: The clip sounds like the word 'air' (realised as a modern British English monophthongal /ɛː/ or centring diphthong /ɛə/).

w.notes: The speaker pronounces the letter H as 'haitch'.
